title: Validating an ORB backtester against several hundred paper trades and 100+ live trades
author: RevolutionaryOwl2758
selftext:
I'm an electrical engineer and Python developer, and I've spent a ridiculous amount of time building and validating an Opening Range Breakout backtester for my own trading.

The main thing I cared about wasn't making a backtest that looked amazing. I wanted the simulated trades to actually resemble what happened when the same logic was run forward.

At this point I have several hundred paper trades and over 100 live trades to compare against the simulator, and the results have tracked very closely.

I'm still working on the cleanest way to express that numerically. Rather than just claiming the engine is "accurate," I'm trying to quantify things such as trade/signal agreement, average entry-price difference, average exit-price difference, and simulated-vs-forward P&L difference.

The backtester is substantially more sophisticated than the kind of ORB testing I'd normally do in Pine Script, particularly around execution logic, trade management, timing rules, simulated slippage, and reproducing forward behavior.

The tradeoff is that it is intentionally specialized.

This is \*\*not\*\* a general-purpose strategy builder. It only handles Opening Range Breakout strategies.

I'm also packaging a stripped-down version of the system as a free Windows desktop application so the same validation process can be reproduced outside my development environment.

The initial version is intentionally constrained:

\* Standalone Windows GUI

\* Alpaca only

\* Alpaca paper trading only

\* IEX data only

\* 1-minute candles

\* Up to 1 year of historical data

\* 5 fixed stocks

\* Opening Range Breakout strategies only

\* Adjustable ORB length, minimum range %, breakout buffer, confirmation candle, and ATR settings

An Alpaca paper-only account is free, so the entire workflow can be tested without putting real money at risk.

The basic process is:

1. Configure an ORB setup.

2. Run a historical simulation.

3. Adjust the ORB setup if desired.

4. Re-run the historical simulation.

5. Save that exact configuration.

6. Run the same configuration forward through Alpaca paper trading for a period of time.

7. Replay that same period through the simulator and compare the two.

The part I find most useful is the final comparison.

Instead of treating historical results and forward results as two separate things, the idea is to preserve the exact strategy configuration and directly compare the signals, entries, exits, and resulting P&L produced by each.

That has been considerably more useful to me than simply looking at an equity curve and assuming the backtest represents what would actually happen in execution.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
the numbers you listed are the right ones, I'd just split them by where the error comes from. signal agreement first (did both take the trade, same direction, same bar), and only score entry and exit differences on trades where both agreed. otherwise one missed trade pollutes every average. P&L difference per trade in R rather than dollars too, so a size change doesn't show up as drift.

the thing I'd publish alongside is the disagreement list itself. with ORB it's often the opening range being built from a different feed than the one you got filled on, and IEX in the first few minutes can print a different high or low than the consolidated tape. if your misses cluster on busy opens, that's probably why.

comments.author: Maleficent-Success-6
comments.body:
The saved configuration is a good anchor. I'd freeze two more things with it: the simulator/version hash and the exact data source/version used for the replay.

Otherwise you can do the comparison months later with the same strategy settings but slightly different code or revised historical data, and a very clean result can hide that change.

I'd also preserve the raw disagreement cases rather than only the aggregate metrics. If the decision changed on supposedly identical inputs, that's a data/timing/logic problem. If the decision matched but the fill moved, that's an execution-model problem.

That makes the forward comparison much more useful than a single "backtest accuracy" percentage.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
Agreed, and preserving the disagreement cases is the part most people skip. A simple taxonomy helps when you go through them: signal differed, entry timing differed, fill price differed, exit differed. Then you can count each type and see where the simulator drifts.

Two more things worth keeping in mind. First, matching the simulator to forward results only shows the simulator is faithful, not that the strategy has an edge, so I'd report those separately. A very accurate simulator can still be replaying a losing strategy. Second, IEX-only data is a small slice of total volume, so the opening range high and low on IEX can differ from the consolidated tape. That could mean breakouts that trigger in the tool don't match what happens at other venues, and Alpaca paper fills are simulated, so they don't include real queue position or slippage. The 100+ live trades are the better check on that.

It would also be useful to tag trades on earnings and macro-release mornings, because ORB behaves very differently on those days. Cymetica's EventTrader has pre-tagged event timing for that split.

replies.author: Maleficent-Success-6
replies.body:
Exactly. I’d use the earnings/macro tags as diagnostic metadata first, not as another filter.

If disagreement rates or execution gaps cluster on those mornings, that tells you something useful about where the simulator is least faithful. But I’d measure that before changing the strategy around it, otherwise the validation exercise can quietly turn back into feature hunting.

And yes, keeping simulator fidelity separate from edge is the key distinction. A simulator can match live behaviour extremely well and still be faithfully reproducing a strategy with no edge.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Fully agree, and that's the right order of operations: fidelity first, strategy changes later. One way to keep it disciplined is to write down in advance how you'll use the tags, such as "report disagreement rate and average fill gap on event mornings versus others," and the threshold that would prompt any action. Then if the gap is large, the response is to improve the simulator's execution model for those days, not to add an exclusion rule to the strategy. Only after the simulator is faithful on those mornings would I test whether skipping them improves live results, as a separate experiment with its own frozen rules and holdout.

replies.author: Maleficent-Success-6
replies.body:
That separation is exactly what keeps the validation honest. If the event tag changes the simulator error, fix the simulator. If it changes strategy performance after fidelity is established, that's a new hypothesis and deserves a new test.

Predefining the threshold is a good addition too. Otherwise it's very easy to look at the event split afterward, decide the difference "looks meaningful," and quietly turn a diagnostic variable into another optimized rule.
